items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the movement of people from the countryside to towns and cities”.
items.answer: Rural-urban migration
items.markingKey: Rural-urban migration: the movement of people from the countryside to towns and cities. [1]

items.stem: Explain the causes of rural-urban migration in LICs.
items.answer: Push: rural poverty, lack of land, mechanisation, drought and environmental degradation, few services, conflict. Pull: perceived jobs in formal and informal sectors, higher wages, schools and hospitals, bright lights, family networks.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per factor up to [4]

items.stem: Explain the consequences of rural-urban migration for the destination city.
items.answer: Rapid growth and informal settlements; pressure on water, sanitation, transport and schools; growth of the informal sector; youthful population; but supply of cheap labour and economic growth.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point [4]

items.stem: Using one named example of rural-urban migration in an LIC or MIC, describe the consequences of the migration for the areas of origin and destination.
items.answer: internal migration in China: Shenzhen grew from about 30 000 (1980) to over 17 million; about 375 million internal migrants by 2020; “left-behind” children (about 60 million) and elderly in villages; urban villages and dormitories; remittances to Sichuan, Anhui and Henan.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 4 marks for accurate, place-specific points (names, dates, figures), max 2 if general. Demographic, economic, social, environmental consequences with figures. [5]

items.stem: Using one named example of rural-urban migration in an LIC or MIC, explain the causes of the migration.
items.answer: rural-urban migration to Dhaka, Bangladesh: River erosion and flooding in districts such as Bhola and Kurigram, landlessness, cyclones and salinity in the south; pull of over 4 million garment-industry jobs; family networks.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 4 marks for accurate, place-specific points (names, dates, figures), max 2 if general. Push and pull factors linked to named places. [5]

items.stem: Briefly explain the causes of the migration, for internal migration in China or another example of rural-urban migration in an LIC or MIC.
items.answer: internal migration in China: Economic reforms from 1978, special economic zones (Shenzhen), factory jobs on the coast, rural incomes about a third of urban; relaxation of hukou controls.

items.stem: “Rural-urban migration benefits source areas more than destination cities.” How far do you agree with this statement? In your answer you may refer to remittances and ageing.
items.answer: For: Remittances, reduced pressure on land and returning skills improve rural livelihoods (Bangladesh, Nepal). Against: Cities gain workers that drive industrial growth (Shenzhen, Dhaka garment industry) but face informal settlements and service pressure; source areas lose young adults, farms are abandoned, families split. Conclusion: Impacts are mixed in both; cities gain most economically, while source areas depend heavily on remittances and suffer demographic loss.

options: The movement of people from the countryside to towns and cities.
The concentration of investment, services and jobs in cities, which encourages rural-urban migration.
A decline in the population of rural areas, usually because of out-migration.
China’s household registration system, which ties access to services to a person’s registered place of origin.

items.stem: Explain the causes of counter-urbanisation.
items.answer: Push from cities (congestion, crime, pollution, high house prices); pull of rural areas (space, quieter environment, cheaper housing); improved transport and IT enabling commuting and teleworking; retirement migration; decentralisation of employment.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per factor [4]

items.stem: Explain why stepped migration occurs.
items.answer: Migrants lack money and information to move directly; smaller towns are closer and offer first jobs and experience; information and contacts are gained before moving to the largest city.

items.stem: Table 14.2 shows population (thousands) in zones of the Paris region in 1971 and 2001: inner city: 882 to 813; outer suburbs: 502 to 540; rural ring within 50 km: 167 to 209; remote rural areas: 175 to 192. Explain how the data provide evidence of counter-urbanisation.
items.answer: Population declined in the inner city and grew fastest in the accessible rural ring, showing movement down the urban hierarchy to smaller settlements beyond the city.

items.answer: (a) Population declined in the inner city and grew fastest in the accessible rural ring, showing movement down the urban hierarchy to smaller settlements beyond the city. (b) They are too far for daily commuting and have fewer services and jobs; young people still leave.

items.stem: Elena argues that counter-urbanisation brings more benefits than problems to rural areas. How far do you agree? Support your answer with examples. In your answer you may refer to services and house prices.
items.answer: For: Newcomers bring spending, skills and renovated housing; schools and some services survive; population decline is reversed. Against: House prices rise beyond local people’s reach; second homes and commuters leave villages empty by day; shops and bus services still close; traffic increases; conflicts over development. Conclusion: The effects depend on the type of incomer and the area: accessible villages may gain, but local young people and services often lose.

items.stem: Explain the reasons for return migration.
items.answer: Achieving savings targets; retirement; family obligations; failure to find work or discrimination; economic improvement at home; changes in immigration rules or recession abroad.

items.stem: A survey of 50 return migrants in a town in central Mexico recorded their main reason for returning: family obligations 7, retirement 22, savings target reached 12, could not find work 6, better opportunities at home 3. Suggest two ways the survey could be improved.
items.answer: Larger or stratified random sample; include returnees from different destinations; allow multiple reasons; pilot the questionnaire; ask about length of time away.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Outline the evidence that supports, and the evidence that challenges, the view that return migration brings greater benefits to source areas than remittances do.
items.answer: For: Returnees bring skills, capital, entrepreneurship and new ideas that create jobs (brain gain). Against: Remittances are larger, regular and reach many more households, funding education and health (Nepal, Philippines); many returnees are elderly or unsuccessful migrants. Conclusion: Remittances provide wider, more regular benefits, but skilled return migration can have a greater long-term effect on development.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the concentration of investment, services and jobs in cities, which encourages rural-urban migration”.
items.answer: Urban bias
items.markingKey: Urban bias: the concentration of investment, services and jobs in cities, which encourages rural-urban migration. [1]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain the positive effects of rural-urban migration on rural source areas. (b) In a class discussion, a student says: “Most urban growth in LICs today is caused by migration alone.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Remittances fund housing, education and farm improvements; reduced pressure on land; returning migrants bring skills and ideas. (b) Not correct. Natural increase in cities now contributes about half or more of urban growth in many LICs.
items.markingKey: (a) [3] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A student writes: “Rural-urban migration only harms rural areas.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) A revision website states: “China’s hukou system has limited migrants’ access to urban services.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Remittances and reduced pressure on land can benefit rural households. (b) Correct. Migrants without local hukou have faced restricted access to schooling, health care and housing.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain the consequences of rural-urban migration for the destination city. (b) In a class discussion, a student says: “Most urban growth in LICs today is caused by migration alone.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Rapid growth and informal settlements; pressure on water, sanitation, transport and schools; growth of the informal sector; youthful population; but supply of cheap labour and economic growth. (b) Not correct. Natural increase in cities now contributes about half or more of urban growth in many LICs.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per point [4] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: The population of Addis Ababa grew from 9.8 million in 2000 to 25.6 million in 2020. Natural increase within the city accounted for 41% of the growth; the rest came from net in-migration. Explain why natural increase contributes a large share of urban growth.
items.answer: Migrants are mostly young adults of child-bearing age; urban death rates are lower than rural; fertility, although lower than rural, remains above replacement.

items.answer: Suburbanisation

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain how the life cycle influences intra-urban migration. (b) A revision website states: “Counter-urbanisation always benefits rural communities.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Young single adults rent near the city centre; families move to suburbs for space and schools; older people may downsize or return to central areas or move to retirement areas. (b) Not correct. House prices rise beyond local people’s reach and some services close as newcomers commute.
items.markingKey: (a) [3] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) In a class discussion, a student says: “The COVID-19 pandemic encouraged some counter-urbanisation in HICs.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain why stepped migration occurs.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Remote working allowed some households to move to smaller towns and rural areas. (b) Migrants lack money and information to move directly; smaller towns are closer and offer first jobs and experience; information and contacts are gained before moving to the largest city.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) [3]

items.stem: With the help of examples, evaluate the claim that counter-urbanisation brings more benefits than problems to rural areas. In your answer you may refer to second homes, house prices and services.
items.answer: For: Newcomers bring spending, skills and renovated housing; schools and some services survive; population decline is reversed. Against: House prices rise beyond local people’s reach; second homes and commuters leave villages empty by day; shops and bus services still close; traffic increases; conflicts over development. Conclusion: The effects depend on the type of incomer and the area: accessible villages may gain, but local young people and services often lose.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “return migration”?
options: Regular back-and-forth movement such as weekly or daily commuting.
Regular movement for part of the year, often to work in harvests or tourism.
The seasonal movement of herders and livestock between summer and winter pastures.
The movement of migrants back to their place of origin after a period living elsewhere.
items.answer: The movement of migrants back to their place of origin after a period living elsewhere.
items.markingKey: Return migration: the movement of migrants back to their place of origin after a period living elsewhere. [1]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) In a class discussion, a student says: “Return migrants can help development in their home areas.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) A student writes: “Circulation involves a permanent change of residence.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Their savings, skills and contacts can create businesses and jobs. (b) Not correct. Circulation is movement that returns to the usual place of residence.

items.answer: (a) 22.5° (b) Positive: savings target, retirement, better opportunities at home; negative: could not find work; family obligations can be either.
